newsitem.title: JAPAN: INTERVIEW--Shiseido takes aim at global rivals.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW--Shiseido takes aim at global rivals.

text.p: Japan's largest beauty products company, Shiseido Co Ltd, is aggressively expanding overseas, aiming to become one of the world's top three cosmetics firms by the year 2005, company officials say.

Shiseido hopes to achieve this feat through a five-year globalisation plan which will boost its annual group net sales to 800 billion yen ($6.77 billion) by the 21st century, with a quarter of the sales coming from abroad.
"We have been enjoying steady growth over the years, but we want to break the pattern and lift sales dramatically," Shisedo director Yasukata Mori told Reuters in a recent interview.
"By the year 2005, we hope we can become one of the world's top three firms," he said.
The L'Oreal Group, Procter & Gamble Co and Unilever currently hold the top three spots in the industry. Shiseido is ranked fourth.

"If we can sustain annual growth of about 30 percent for our existing overseas businesses, we should be able to secure 120 billion yen ($1.01 billion) (in overseas sales)," said the company's chief executive officer, Akira Genma. "The remainder will come from new businesses."

In the 1996/97 business year ended in March, overseas sales surged 28 percent to 64.5 billion yen ($546 million), while total group sales rose by about five percent to 588.6 billion yen ($4.98 billion).

The firm has been living up to its ambitious plans, recently adding Helene Curtis Industries Inc's hair salon unit and Carter-Wallace Inc's skincare products plant to its list of assets. It has also unveiled plans to launch sales in new markets such as Vietnam and Colombia.
Investors have applauded the recent moves, lifting Shiseido's shares by about 50 percent since the start of the calendar year.
Mori said that Shiseido was interested in the potential of the Asian market, in which demand for cosmetics is expected to grow by $1 billion annually.

"There are worries about Asian currencies and investment in the region but U.S. and European firms vying for market share will also face the same risks that we do," said Mori, who also heads up Shiseido's international headquarters.
"Asia has much potential and changes quickly and we cannot afford to sit back and wait," he said. "We try to minimise risks by expanding our business through joint ventures."

In an effort to chip away at the market share of cosmetics giants such as Procter & Gamble's Max Factor, the firm is planning to launch a new skincare and make-up line in September targeting Asia's rapidly growing middle class.

"We hope to complete the introduction of new brands by 1999, although we have no time limit for mergers and acquisitions," said Mori, "We will continue to look into the possibilities of business with new partners to the year 2000."
Although Asia, especially China, has the largest growth potential, company officials say it is also extremely important that the firm expand further in Europe and the United States.

"France is the centre of fashion and has great influence all over the world and to succeed there is strategically important," Mori said. "The U.S. cosmetics market is the largest in the world and many trends are set there."

By the year 2000, Shiseido expects 40 percent of sales to come from Asia, while the United States and Europe will each account for 30 percent. At the moment the three regions' shares are 34 percent, 20 percent and 38 percent, respectively, with the remainder coming from duty-free sales.
In order to ensure that its ambitious overseas expansion plan goes smoothly, Shiseido is forming regional headquarters in Europe, United States and Asia.

"Although we don't have any concrete plans to do so at the moment, we want to have the flexibility, should the need arise, to form a holding company or to list our firms on overseas bourses," Genma added. ($1=118 yen)
